title: AlphaFold
matchup: Jumper et al. (2021, AlphaFold 2) vs Baldi and Pollastri (2002), Hochreiter et al. (2007) and Golkov et al. (2016)
question: Did the 2021 AlphaFold 2 paper omit earlier work that should have been cited for its protein-structure prediction method?

usual_credit.summary: John Jumper and colleagues presented AlphaFold 2 in Nature in 2021 after its CASP14 evaluation. The paper describes an end-to-end system that uses multiple sequence alignments, pair representations and a structure module to predict atomic coordinates, with accuracy competitive with experimental structures in many test cases. The 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry awarded half the prize jointly to Demis Hassabis and Jumper for protein structure prediction, while David Baker received the other half for protein design. The Nobel Committee distinguishes AlphaFold 2's redesigned architecture from AlphaFold 1.

claim.summary: Schmidhuber argues that AlphaFold 2 omitted relevant neural-network predecessors: Baldi and Pollastri's 2002 protein-analysis pipeline, Hochreiter, Heusel and Obermayer's 2007 LSTM work on protein homology, and Golkov and colleagues' 2016 contact-map predictor using co-evolution statistics. He regards the use of alignment-derived inputs and learned structural predictions as the relevant continuity, and describes the later system as changing the network and prediction target while using more data and compute. His claim is that these relationships warranted citations, not that the earlier papers reported AlphaFold 2's atomic-coordinate accuracy.

response.summary: The AlphaFold 2 paper presents its contribution as an end-to-end architecture that predicts atomic coordinates and performs well even without a closely related known structure. It cites earlier neural protein-structure work, including Qian and Sejnowski (1988), Fariselli and colleagues (2001), and later contact-map methods, but not the three papers Schmidhuber names. The Nobel Committee likewise acknowledges neural secondary-structure prediction by 1988 while describing AlphaFold 2 as a redesigned system. These are the authors' and committee's accounts of the contribution, rather than a direct reply to Schmidhuber's citation complaint.

agreed_facts: Jumper et al. published "Highly accurate protein structure prediction with AlphaFold" in Nature in 2021, and the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry gave a quarter each to Hassabis and Jumper.
Baldi and Pollastri published "A machine learning strategy for protein analysis" in IEEE Intelligent Systems in 2002, and Golkov et al. presented their contact prediction paper at NeurIPS in 2016.

The reference list of the 2021 AlphaFold paper includes Qian and Sejnowski (1988) and Fariselli et al. (2001) on neural networks for protein structure, and it does not include Baldi and Pollastri (2002), Hochreiter et al. (2007) or Golkov et al. (2016).

The Nobel Committee's background text says that neural networks had entered secondary structure prediction as early as 1988 and that AlphaFold 2 abandoned the convolutional design of AlphaFold 1 for a Transformer architecture.
crux: The sources differ on whether the earlier pipelines, which fed alignment-derived profiles or co-evolution statistics into neural networks, contain the ideas that AlphaFold 2 rests on, or whether its end-to-end Evoformer and structure module are a new design for which that earlier work is background. They also differ on whether the 2021 authors should have cited it.

card.headline: AlphaFold 2
card.question: Should the AlphaFold 2 paper have cited earlier neural protein-prediction work it left out?
card.claim: He says AlphaFold 2 built on uncited neural protein work by Baldi and Pollastri (2002), Hochreiter et al. (2007) and Golkov et al. (2016).
card.pushback: The Nobel Committee calls AlphaFold 2 neural network engineering with a multitude of new inventions, and its paper cites other early neural protein work.
card.crux: The question is whether the 2002-2016 networks contain AlphaFold 2's core ideas or are only background to a new design.
